after: ## Key idea 1: the arithmetic of change
alt: A population box with births and immigrants flowing in and deaths and emigrants flowing out. Below, three equations: natural change equals birth rate minus death rate and can be negative; net migration equals immigrants minus emigrants; total change equals natural change plus net migration. A warning notes that infant mortality is per 1,000 live births.
caption: Births, deaths and migration: the only three ways a population changes.

after: ## Key idea 2: why the world's population grew so fast
alt: A schematic graph: the death rate falls first while the birth rate stays high, and falls only later; the shaded gap between them is rapid growth. Reasons deaths fell: better food supply, clean water and sewage disposal, vaccination and antibiotics, hygiene knowledge. Births lag because family decisions change over a generation. A timeline marks about 1 billion people around 1800, 7 billion in 2011 and 8 billion in November 2022.
caption: Death rates fell before birth rates did; the gap drove the boom.

after: ## Key idea 3: contrasting rates of natural change
alt: Five factor groups, each with what pushes the birth rate up and down. Economic: children as farm workers and old-age support versus the cost of children in cities. Social: early marriage and low status of women versus women in education and work. Health: high versus low infant mortality and contraception. Cultural and religious: valuing large families versus smaller family norms. Political: pro-natalist versus anti-natalist policy.
caption: Group the factors, then say which way each pushes the rate.

alt: Three balances of people against resources. Over-population: the people side is heavier, with food shortages, unemployment and overcrowding; Bangladesh is often used as an example. Optimum: balanced, giving the highest standard of living. Under-population: the resources side is heavier, with labour shortages and unused land or minerals; Australia is often used. A note says density alone is not over-population, as the Netherlands shows.
caption: Over- and under-population compare people with resources, not with area.

alt: A timeline: the one-child policy around 1979 to 1980, relaxed to two children from 2016 and three in 2021. Four evaluation steps: growth slowed but the birth rate was already falling; unintended consequences of more boys than girls, rapid ageing and the 4-2-1 family; human rights concerns over coercion; and an overall judgement of effective but costly. A diagram shows four grandparents, two parents and one adult child who may have to support all six.
caption: Judge a policy against its aims, its side effects and its acceptability.

alt: A birth rate of 32 per 1,000 minus a death rate of 9 gives natural change of 23 per 1,000, or 2.3 per cent. Adding net migration of minus 2 gives total change of 21 per 1,000, or 2.1 per cent. Multiplying by a population of 40 million and dividing by 1,000 gives a yearly increase of 840,000 people.
caption: Natural change, then add migration, then scale up to the population.
